Wave 2: pantry onto the engine (aspect-engine ticket 21)
aspect-engine 21
86f8893 · 6 files
Carve doc first (docs/architecture/wave2-carve-2026-08-23.md). Headline finding: unlike notes/lists/places, pantry has no quarantine state anywhere in its Room schema - the reconciliation gate runs entirely upstream (PantryReceiptAgent.parseAndReconcile returns Quarantined without ever touching Room), so every legacy row is gate-reconciled by construction and migrates with provenance unconditionally LLM_RECONCILED, never USER. PantryAspectSeeder: Pantry aspect, Receipt + LineItem record types. LineItem.receipt is a REFERENCE to Receipt with DeletePolicy.CASCADE - the first real aspect to use the engine's REFERENCE/delete-policy machinery (previously exercised only by RecordStoreTest's synthetic schemas). Receipt.total and LineItem.totalPrice are each wired as primaryAmountFieldId (the first seeder to promote an amount column; Wave 1 only ever promoted a due-date column). Macro estimate fields are named with an explicit 'estimated' prefix (estimatedCaloriesKcal etc) since FieldDef carries no separate description column - the field NAME is the only user-facing string this schema layer has, and CLAUDE.md §4 rule 5 requires it say estimate. EngineDataMigrationWave2: idempotent copier (completion flag + per-row guid backstop, guids reused directly from PantryReceipt/PantryLineItem.syncId - both already carried one). Copies every receipt first, keeps a legacy-id -> engine-id map, then copies each receipt's line items through that map so a REFERENCE field is never asked to point at a not-yet-created parent. Neither entity carries an insert-time clock, so both engine clocks are seeded from purchaseDate (stated as a deliberate substitution in the carve doc, not a bug). Added PantryReceiptDao.getAll() - a plain additive @Query the copier needs for a complete, unlimited pass over the legacy table; no schema/version change. Old pantry tables, PantryController, and all three LiveToolbox pantry tools (import_receipt, list_recent_groceries, get_grocery_spend) are untouched and keep working - cutover is a later wave. The carve doc names which of those die into meta-tools at cutover and leaves get_grocery_spend's per-currency-aggregate shape as an open question rather than guessing. Tests: PantryAspectSeederTest (6) - idempotence, primaryAmountFieldId wiring on both record types, no primaryDueDateFieldId on Receipt, REFERENCE/CASCADE config, estimate-field naming and non-required/non-locked status, currency CHOICE options. EngineDataMigrationWave2Test (8) - count-exact, content-faithful (money cents exact, macros carried, reference intact, absent vs null unit price), CASCADE delete verified through RecordStore.delete, provenance asserted LLM_RECONCILED, idempotence at both the flag and per-row layers, zero-line-item receipt. Suite green both key ways (with and without -Pnokey).

MUST-FIX 1 - cross-device creates: records.guid (v37) is the mirror's identity column now, never EngineRecord.id. ALTER TABLE + per-row UUID backfill (SQLite randomblob evaluated fresh per row) + unique index, byte-confirmed against the generated 37.json. RecordStore.create takes an optional guid (defaults to a fresh UUID; MirrorSync passes the foreign row's own guid when materializing a record born on another device, so a re-export keeps the identical guid). MirrorCodec drops the id column entirely and writes/reads guid instead. MirrorSync.mergeRecordSheet now has three cases: blank guid creates fresh, non-blank guid with no local match CREATES (preserving the guid and the row's own provenance) instead of quarantining, non-blank guid with a local match merges as before. widget_instances/muted_reminders keep referencing local ids on purpose - neither is exported by the mirror, so the cross-device problem does not apply to them (documented in EngineRecord's own doc comment). The same per-device-id gap exists in theory for aspectId/recordTypeId/fieldDefId and is flagged, not fixed - out of this review's scope. MUST-FIX 2 - wired the promised triggers for real. RecordStore gained a companion-level afterWrite SharedFlow (every call site builds its own instance, so this had to be class-level to be heard by all of them) that fires after every successful create/update/delete/restore. New MirrorLifecycleBinder subscribes it to scheduleExport, and hooks ProcessLifecycleOwner (new lifecycle-process dependency) so app foreground imports and app background exports. Registered once from MidnightApplication.onCreate, inside the existing Robolectric-gated block, gated on a mirror folder being configured. MirrorFolderPreferences.init moved from the debug activity into Application so the binder sees live state from process start. SHOULD-FIX 3 - export now imports FIRST, always. The old order wrote Room's current state over the file before ever looking at it, so a hand edit made since the last look was blind-overwritten with no quarantine - the read-back hash then matched itself and the trailing import found nothing to merge. exportAllAndImport calls importAll before building any export bytes. SHOULD-FIX 4 - MirrorSyncActivity states in words that the spreadsheet's dropdowns/highlighting are decoration and the import gate is the real check. Tests: foreign-guid-with-no-local-match creates (the exact broken case), both-sides-changed-since-export asserts the file-wins branch directly, a provenance-preserved-on-foreign-create case, and a full create-on-A/import-to- B/re-export-from-B round trip confirming the guid survives unchanged while local ids differ on each side. 24 mirror tests total (7 codec, 17 merge), all green. Build the xlsx mirror and its sync (ticket 20)
no ticket
42dbce3 · 10 files
MirrorCodec: pure records<->xlsx bytes codec via fastexcel, one workbook per aspect, one sheet per record type plus a _definitions sheet. Fixed header contract (id/createdAt/updatedAt/provenance + one column per field), money as integer cents, dates as integer epoch millis, computed columns never read back. DETERMINISTIC/LLM_RECONCILED rows carry a (read-only) provenance suffix. Generated dataValidation rules are decoration only (fastexcel 0.19.0 has no per-cell lock API - traced against its source); the import gate is the real enforcement. MirrorStore: SAF layer over a user-picked tree URI. Write is always a full rwt rewrite, read back and sha256-verified; a mismatch quarantines that one aspect's mirror in words (MirrorStateStore), never the whole folder. MirrorFolderPreferences persists the tree URI, matching ledger's own pattern but with its own read+write grant. MirrorSync: debounced export after RecordStore writes plus an immediate exportNow for app-background; import on app foreground and after export. Import gate gives every row a worded quarantine reason (field parse error, illegal choice value, dangling reference via RecordStore itself). Binding row-level merge keyed by record id + updatedAt, latest wins, documented concrete tie-break for the case Sheets can't signal (a hand edit that never bumps updatedAt). Reconciled rows rejected as read-only. Remote delete: locally-absent rows older than the last export stamp are trashed through RecordStore, never a raw DAO write. Definitions sheet merge is bounded to existing unlocked fields' name/required/position - creating a brand-new aspect/type/field purely from a spreadsheet row is out of scope, and every such row surfaces as a named warning rather than being silently dropped. MirrorSyncActivity: debug-only settings stub (WidgetPagerActivity's own adb-launch pattern) - pick folder, sync now, per-aspect last-sync/quarantine state. This is also the on-A25 write-back probe ticket 01 left owed; see the report for the exact steps. fastexcel 0.19.0 (writer + reader) added to the version catalog - plain-JVM, no Robolectric needed, confirmed by MirrorCodecTest actually running bare. 19 new tests (6 codec round-trip, 13 merge/gate semantics), full suite green both -Pnokey and with a key. No Room migration - the engine tables already cover everything this needs.

5157471 · 12 files
Nine meta-tools (EngineToolbox.kt, LiveToolbox delegates to it): list_aspects, describe_aspect, query_records, create_record, update_record, delete_record, aspect_clerk, create_aspect, update_aspect. RecordStore stays the only write door for EngineRecord rows; schema tools (create_aspect/update_aspect) write Aspect/RecordType/FieldDef directly, gated behind a confirm handshake (stashDraft/takeDraft) so nothing commits on the first call. - delete_record: single id trashes immediately with a spoken receipt; a query-matched bulk delete returns the count and commits nothing until a second call with confirm: true. - aspect_clerk: SubAgent executor on the default Flash tier, bounded investigate loop over the six read/write meta-tools, handed the grounded wall clock + UTC offset in its system instruction per ticket 07's carried- forward requirement (never let it guess 'today'). Reports rows written/ failed in words per the outcome rule. - create_aspect/update_aspect: schema draft comes from a Pro-tier (gemini-3.1-pro-preview) generator subagent via structured output; commit only on a confirmed second call with the same draftToken. - Every description carries the outcome rule (failure states in words what did not happen) and the estimate rule (never guess a value the user did not give); none call the user 'the driver' (PromptRoleNamingTest stays green). Tests: EngineToolboxTest (Robolectric, the six directly-dispatched tools against a real CarDatabase), EngineToolboxClerkResultTest (clerk's five outcome branches, no network), EngineToolboxDraftHandshakeTest (confirm handshake's token state machine, no network). Fix row/col swap at the move-commit call site; extract pointer-to-cell mapping
no ticket
ac3f032 · 3 files
Sixth feel-test pass, Kevin reproduced over adb with screenshots: dragging ANY full-width card any distance in any direction always committed at row 0, col 0. ROOT CAUSE, exact location: DeckGrid.kt's onMoveDragEnd computed the commit candidate with two adjacent, UNNAMED run { } blocks passed positionally into GridEngine.clampMoveTarget(item, targetRow, targetCol, columnCount). The FIRST block - landing in the targetRow slot - computed a COLUMN value (built from colPitchPx/originCol/accumPx.x). The SECOND block - landing in targetCol - computed a ROW value (built from rowPitchPx/originRow/accumPx.y). Row and column were transposed at that one call site. Why it always read as (0,0): clampMoveTarget clamps targetCol into [0, columnCount - colSpan]. For a FULL-width card that range is exactly [0, 0], so whatever value the swap put in the targetCol slot clamped to 0 regardless of magnitude - and the swap put the near-zero column value (unchanged from originCol, since every reproduction was a vertical-only drag on a card already at column 0) into targetRow, which floors at 0 and stayed ~0. Two independent near-misses that both happened to land on 0 for every widget in the reproduction, since all of them are full-width and start at column 0. The live preview computation a few lines above (the drag's own on-screen ghost outline) did the identical arithmetic CORRECTLY, named its results candidateRow/candidateCol, and passed them in the right order - only the commit path, which duplicated the arithmetic inline instead of reusing one implementation, got the order wrong. That is why the preview outline looked right during the drag while the drop still reverted: two different, divergent computations of the same value. FIX, per the brief's three-part demand: 1. Root cause found and fixed at the exact line (the onMoveDragEnd call site's two run { } blocks, now replaced with a single named, correctly-ordered destructure). 2. JVM test added that would have caught it: GridGestureTest."dragging DOWN increases row, column unchanged - the exact shape that broke" reproduces the precise symptom shape (vertical- only drag, origin column 0) and asserts row and column land independently, never conflated. 3. The pointer-to-cell mapping is now its OWN pure function, GridGesture.candidateCell(originRow, originCol, accumPxX, accumPxY, colPitchPx, rowPitchPx) -> Pair<row, col>, in GridModel.kt (zero Compose imports, same as every other function in that file). Both the live preview and the commit call this SAME function now - there is exactly one implementation of this arithmetic left anywhere, so there is nothing left to diverge. GridGestureTest covers up/down/left/right/diagonal, sub-cell jitter that stays inside a pitch band (must not move), sub-cell jitter that crosses a boundary (must move), row floored at 0, column deliberately NOT floored (clamping is the caller's job), non-zero origin, and an explicit "row from Y, col from X, never swapped" case. This is the third consecutive pass to ship a gesture-math bug invisible to the JVM suite because the arithmetic lived inline in Compose code - it now has direct coverage, leaving only pointer EVENT PLUMBING (detectDragGestures wiring, state threading) as the honest remainder no JVM test can reach. compileDebugKotlin, testDebugUnitTest (both key ways), assembleDebug all green.

Fifth feel-test pass, Kevin plus a screenshot, three defects: 1. DROP DOES NOT STICK IN EMPTY SPACE. Confirmed cause: baseItems was remember(items.toList(), columnCount) { GridEngine.normalize(items, columnCount) }. Fixing the fourth-pass bug (remember never invalidating) made baseItems recompute for real on every content change for the first time - which made GridEngine.normalize's own unconditional compact() visible for the first time too. normalize is correct and intentional for untrusted FIRST input (a raw widget_instances read, hand-typed fixtures) but was never meant to run on an already-committed, already-valid layout - compact() with no pinned id pulls a deliberately-gapped layout upward on every single call, so every commit's own recomposition immediately re-compacted the card the user just placed in an empty space. JVM test written FIRST, documents the exact mechanism: GridEngineTest."normalize does NOT round-trip a valid gapped layout untouched" - a two-item collision-free layout with a deliberate gap, run through normalize, is NOT bit-identical (the gapped item gets pulled up). This test passes against the unmodified GridEngine (normalize's own behavior was never the bug - it is correct for what it is; calling it repeatedly was the bug). Traced end to end: DeckGrid.kt's baseItems val, computed every recomposition once the fourth-pass fix made the remember key real, called GridEngine.normalize -> compact(settled, pinnedId = null) -> pulled every gapped item to the top of its column. That is the exact function moving the card. Fix: normalize now runs EXACTLY ONCE per DeckGrid instance (the accepted "one-shot flag" idiom - a remembered boolean flips true-to-false on the very first composition and never again). Every recomposition after that trusts `items` verbatim, no processing at all - a value that already round-tripped through this component's own commit path (displaceForPlacement, clampMoveTarget, clampResizeTarget) is already valid, and reprocessing it is exactly what silently relocated the user's own placement. 2. HALF-WIDTH CHROME BROKEN (screenshot: "LOG A DRIVE // QU" truncated by the opaque remove chip drawn on top, not by ellipsis). The chip and resize handle are drawn by DeckGrid.kt's GridCellChrome, layered on top of the caller's own DeckPane - DeckPane has no idea either exists, so its pill's own ellipsis clamp (paneWidth - 16dp) was computed against the FULL card width, with no awareness that a 28dp opaque chip sits on top of the last ~30-40dp of it. On a half-width card with a two-clause title, the pill legitimately rendered text (with its own ellipsis) reaching into the chip's zone, and the chip visually swallowed the ellipsis dots along with the last few characters. Fixed by reserving a CHIP_CLEARANCE (36dp) off the trailing edge of `content()` itself, edit mode only - so DeckPane's own ellipsis point, and any right-reaching content inside it (DeckButton's fill width), naturally stop clear of where the chip and handle actually sit. Does not touch DeckPane (shared production component used across many existing screens) at all. 3. CONTENT CLIPPING (agenda card's third row sliced mid-glyph at the card's bottom edge). Two-part fix: (a) DeckGrid's own per-cell Box now carries Modifier.clipToBounds() as a structural, defensive guarantee - any widget whose content overflows its assigned rowSpan now cuts cleanly at the card's own boundary instead of bleeding a half-visible glyph past it; (b) the actual overflowing mocks are fixed at the source - PrototypeGrid.kt's initialGridItems now assigns AGENDA and RECORD_LIST kinds (both render three DeckRows, 144dp, plus header/padding chrome) two rows tall instead of one, which comfortably fits all three rows without needing the clip at all in practice. compileDebugKotlin, testDebugUnitTest (both key ways), assembleDebug all green.

Fourth feel-test verdict: "doesnt commit, i drop card to new position but it snaps back to old position." ROOT CAUSE (confirmed): baseItems was remember(items, columnCount) { GridEngine.normalize(items, columnCount) }, keyed directly on items. The harness's items is a SnapshotStateList mutated IN PLACE (clear() + addAll(), never replaced with a new instance). remember's change-check compares the new key against the previously stored key via equals() - since both are literally the SAME mutated object, the comparison degenerates to x.equals(x), which is trivially true regardless of what the list now holds. baseItems froze at whatever it computed on DeckGrid's very first composition and never recomputed again: every card rendered its pre-drag position forever, and every settle animation's target was that same frozen position. onLayoutChange correctly updated the caller's own state the whole time - DeckGrid's own baseItems just never noticed. Coordinator's hypothesis (a self-overlap flaw in GridEngine.displaceForPlacement, the mover's own old position counting as an obstacle to itself) was checked FIRST via a new GridEngineTest case - "a short move whose candidate overlaps the mover's OWN old cells still commits, mover excluded" - and PASSES against the existing code, disproving it at the GridEngine layer: others already filters it.id != candidate.id before any collision check runs. The bug lived entirely in DeckGrid.kt's own composition, not in the pure model - stated plainly per the Compose-plumbing precedent from the first feel-test pass's resize-commit bug. Fix: key on items.toList() instead of items - a genuinely new immutable copy taken fresh every recomposition, so remember's equals check compares real structural List content against a frozen snapshot from last time, never an object against itself. Fixes move AND resize identically, since both share the same baseItems value - no separate resize-specific flaw existed. Deferred polish added in the same pass: displaced occupants now animate to their new cells with the same 200ms settle the actively dragged/resized card gets, instead of jumping. displacementSettle is a map keyed by id (an Animatable per currently-settling occupant) rather than a single shared Animatable, since one drop's knock-on chain can displace more than one occupant at once; startDisplacementSettles is called from both onMoveDragEnd and onResizeDragEnd right after a valid commit, guarding against a stale coroutine clobbering a newer settle for the same id. compileDebugKotlin, testDebugUnitTest (both key ways), assembleDebug all green.

Fourth feel-test verdict: 'feels better. but it doesnt replace or move the items in the grid up if something is already there.' Snap model stays; occupied-target behavior changes from REJECT to DISPLACE. 1. New GridEngine.displaceForPlacement(items, candidate, columnCount): the candidate is always accepted exactly as proposed, and whatever it overlaps relocates to the nearest free space, searching upward first (closest row above, then columns left to right), then downward (candidate's own row and below) when upward is exhausted. Only actual overlapped occupants (plus any dependent chain through processing order) move; anything the candidate and its chain never touched stays bit-identical. Returns null only when genuinely impossible - a displaced occupant's own colSpan wider than columnCount (row search is unbounded, column width is not) or the candidate itself out of bounds. 2. DeckGrid.kt's drag/resize commit path now calls displaceForPlacement instead of commitIfValid. overlapsAny/commitIfValid (the second generation's outright-reject pair) are kept, doc-marked unused by the interactive path - same posture as moveTo/resize/resolveCollisions/ compact from the earlier rework. 3. Preview honesty: while hovering a spot that would displace, every occupant that would actually move is shown as a chrome-dim ghost outline at its would-be new cell, computed from the SAME displaceForPlacement call the eventual commit uses, so the drop can never differ from what was previewed. The candidate's own outline stays chrome-text (valid) or quarantine (the null/impossible case) - that null case is now the ONLY thing that still triggers the error-tone-and-animate-home rejection. 4. Out-of-bounds candidate clamping is unchanged (clampMoveTarget/ clampResizeTarget still run before displaceForPlacement). 5. GridEngineTest: 12 new displaceForPlacement cases - no-op when nothing overlaps, single occupant moved to the nearest free row above, moves down when upward is exhausted, finds a free column at the same row before changing rows, two simultaneously-colliding occupants chained through processing order, a defensive case for the (provably unreachable under this construction, kept as a safety net) knock-on requeue branch, null on an occupant whose own colSpan cannot fit any column, null on an out-of-bounds candidate, no-op-wrapped-non-null on an unknown id, and bit-identical untouched items. Known scope cut, stated rather than hidden: displaced OTHER occupants land at their new cell without their own settle animation - only the actively dragged/resized card gets one, carried over from the prior pass. His record existed - Jeep, 227,374 mi, 12 Aug, not deleted - while the maintenance clock said 227,483 with a null date, so the Service History screen showed a service the assistant denied out loud. Untick did not undo the log, so a mis-tick corrected on the checklist stayed forever in the training history and every voice answer - and unreachably, since the row is backdated and undo_last_log selects the most recent. It gates both the immediate and the delayed reconnect, and the delayed one re-checks after its delay because the delay can itself carry the last interaction out of the window. It composes with the existing prewarm-failure backoff rather than replacing it: a dead key and an idle app are different failures wanting different guards. The three cold paths are untouched, so a tap, a wake word and a proactive raise all still connect from a fully closed socket. The raise path is traced rather than tested, and says so: requestSpeak with no session falls to startProactive, which builds a session and speaks on Connected. A silent raise would be a worse bug than the churn, which is why it was checked rather than assumed. The trade is real and is in the code comments: the first thing said after a long idle pays a cold connect, about a second more than warm, once per idle stretch instead of 565 times a day. goal-plans 01goal-plans 02

goal-plans ticket 01. Position stands, meta-analyses and government guidance only - findings with per-claim citations, plus the draft playbook ticket 02 will lift into a PrimingTopic. TWO NUMBERS ARE GENUINELY CONTESTED, AND NEITHER IS A ROUNDING DETAIL The ISSN's 2.3-3.1 g/kg protein figure for hypocaloric periods traces back to a source that states it per kg of LEAN mass, inside a document whose other positions use total bodyweight. For a lean person the two are close. At ~35% body fat they differ by about a third - the gap between a sane target and an unreachable one. And 0.5-1.0% bodyweight per week is the recommended rate, but the evidence for its top end comes from lean, resistance-trained athletes. Whether someone carrying more fat can safely lose faster is not established. Settled decision 5 said say-it-once rather than hedge forever. These two are the exception: contested in the literature rather than merely estimated, so the playbook states the disagreement instead of picking a side. TWO THINGS IT REFUSES TO INVENT There is no established point where added volume reverses hypertrophy - the meta-regressions show flattening, not a downturn. Any specific "junk volume" number is secondary-source folklore and the playbook says not to invent one. And kettlebells have never been equated against barbell training for hypertrophy. Kevin's own example turns out to have the weakest evidence base of anything asked about, so the playbook recommends them as reasonable and says plainly that no meta-analysis backs the equivalence. The substitution gaps - loaded knee flexion, vertical pull without an anchor, heavy hinge past the point bodyweight reaches failure inside thirty reps - are reasoned from the load-independence precondition rather than tested directly, and are tagged that way in both documents. A recommender claiming a home gym has no gaps would be overclaiming. The kidney boundary is the sharpest refusal: CKD guidance is 0.55-0.80 g/kg/day, directly contradicting every protein recommendation in the doctrine. That is why it must be a refusal and a referral rather than a quietly halved number. Also updates L32. Worktree isolation was tried per that lesson's own rule and FAILED: a fresh worktree has no local.properties, that file is gitignored, and it holds sdk.dir - so neither agent could run gradle at all, and both stalled fighting it. Their code was fine and dropped straight into the main tree. Copy local.properties into any worktree before dispatching an agent that must build. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Nine settled decisions, five tickets, and goal-keeping ticket 01 closed as SUPERSEDED rather than resolved - no decision was made about what "on track" means, and recording one would leave a phantom answer for someone to find. It carries forward as fog, and it gets easier once a plan exists, because the plan states the target rather than the goal implying one. THE HALF THAT IS EASY TO MISS "accept recommended with user being able to tweak the plan or ask the agent - hey i dont have access to a gym, can we mix in kettlebell workouts etc." That is half the destination, not a later nicety. A plan you can only accept or reject is a generator; a plan you can talk to is a coach. It is ticket 03 and it carries the harder open questions - where a stated constraint lives so he never has to say "no gym" twice, and what happens when a revision contradicts the doctrine ("cut to 800 calories"), where the refusal has to be the feature. WHAT THIS REUSES RATHER THAN BUILDS Kevin asked for a recommender with "skills that can be audited and edited". That already ships: PrimingTopic and PlaybookStore are user-editable doctrine with requiredPhrases guards that refuse an edit deleting a safety boundary. A new BIO-shaped topic joins the existing four and the auditable half needs no new code. Two stores of editable doctrine is how two subtly different safety rules end up shipping. Writes go through set_meal_target, set_sleep_target, create_workout_plan and set_goal - all already in the advisor's writable-op allowlist. Nothing new gets write access. RESEARCH ONCE, NOT AT RUNTIME Kevin called the research a ticket, and it is - fired now. But it runs ONCE and becomes the shipped playbook text, rather than the recommender searching the web per plan. A plan must be reproducible and auditable; one depending on what a search returned that morning is neither, and health guidance is where a bad source does the most harm. HONESTY WITHOUT NAGGING An LLM calorie target is a guess dressed as a number, and CLAUDE.md sec 4 rule 5 says say so. But saying "estimated" every day trains him to stop hearing it. So it is said ONCE, at generation, and after acceptance they are targets he chose. The failure being chased is the model asserting something its tools did not return, and that is visible from tool names and the assistant's own words. It never needed the mail text. Reuse the existing flag; two notions of read-through is how one gets checked in half the places. WHY NOT "KEEP ONLY INTERESTING TURNS" Offered and rejected, and the reason is the whole point of the ticket: the 142k turn looked like an ordinary successful turn. No error, no refusal, no tool failure. A filter tuned to interesting-looking turns would have dropped the single most important record in the app's history. Mic ownership: ONE arbiter object, priority live turn > ring listening > wake word. An object rather than written-down rules precisely because written-down rules enforced at N call sites is the shape that failed today - the `ducked` boolean stayed true after Android took audio focus and the assistant spoke inaudibly for a whole session. The folder is the truth and is re-read every time, deliberately NOT using the ledger's import tracking: that pattern is for immutable statements, and these documents are mutable by design. Memory decay: importance times age, applied on recall, deleting nothing. A wrong curve then costs relevance rather than data - hard expiry loses something he wanted with no way to know it happened. Ticket 02 of the location-intelligence map. Four keyless hazard sources behind ONE tool with a category parameter, plus get_reported_crime_history as its own tool. 99 voice tools now. 1875 tests green. EVERY ENDPOINT WAS HIT LIVE, NOT CODED AGAINST DOCS The response shapes drove the parsers. That is the difference between this and the AirNow client we deliberately did not write, and it paid for itself four times: USGS puts coordinates as [lon, lat, depth] and its free-text "place" is not reliable for a consistent spoken distance, so bearing and distance are computed from geometry rather than read from prose. NIFC needed IncidentTypeCategory='WF' or prescribed burns come back as wildfires. That field carries NO published domain, so the code set is empirically observed and the comment says so rather than implying otherwise. FBI CDE keys its monthly series by "<Agency Name> Offenses" - a dynamic key found by its suffix, never hardcoded - and the latest year present is usually incomplete, trailing nulls. So "most recent complete year" is computed, never assumed. That is the ticket's honesty requirement surviving contact with real data rather than being a nice sentence in a description. Geocoder.adminArea returns "Texas" while FEMA and FBI both filter on "TX", and Android has no API for that conversion. Hence UsStates.kt. THE CRIME TOOL IS THE POINT is_area_safe does not exist and will not. The description states in words that the data is agency-level rather than neighborhood, roughly 13 months stale, voluntarily reported and incomplete, and does not answer whether a place is safe. Asked that, it says so and offers the historical figure instead. A named place matching no agency returns null rather than silently answering about the nearest one - answering about the wrong jurisdiction is worse than not answering. HONEST SIMPLIFICATIONS, RECORDED FEMA is filtered by state, not county; resolving a county to FEMA's numeric fipsCountyCode needs a table this ticket did not scope. The output names the actual designatedArea, so nothing claims more locality than it has. AIR is deliberately absent and commented as such - AirNow is blocked on ticket 10's login visit. FIXES AN INCONSISTENCY I CREATED When I committed geofences, the pre-commit hook regenerated docs/voice.html and README.md from the WORKING TREE, which held this agent's uncommitted copy. So dev has been documenting two tools whose source was not committed. This commit makes the docs true again. The real lesson is about parallel builds, not the hook: two agents in one checkout also produced two spurious Gradle failures today (a stopped daemon, a vanished results file). Filed as a lesson rather than left as folklore. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Geofences that actually fire, and the double-announce they would have caused
location-intelligence 05
2f0d116 · 14 files
Ticket 05 of the location-intelligence map. Real OS geofences replace the raw distance math on GPS polls, which is what makes place reminders fire when the app is closed rather than depending on a poll happening to land near the place. Nearest-80 of Android's 100 cap, re-registered on the existing 20s arrival poll rather than a second timer, and re-registered from BootReceiver because geofences do not survive a reboot. THE BEST PART WAS NOT ASKED FOR Arrival handling was private inside AriaForegroundService. It is now ArrivalController.onArrived, so the geofence receiver and the GPS poll call ONE function instead of two copies that would have drifted. Any future arrival signal calls that. A FORK THE BUILD SURFACED RATHER THAN IMPROVISED Both signals now converge on that one handler with no debounce - and on a real arrival both will usually fire, seconds apart. That is the same reminder read out twice for one arrival. The build flagged it and stopped, which was right. Resolved with claimAnnouncement(place, now): check-and-claim in ONE step, because the geofence runs on a broadcast thread and the poll on the service scope, and a separate check-then-stamp would let both pass before either stamped. Five tests, including that a second announcement re-arms the window instead of leaving it open. AND A BUG FOUND WHILE IN THERE The raise used ruleId "place_arrival" for every place, so brushing off the reminder at the gym would have silenced arrivals at work and home for a day. Now per-place. That is the second time today a shared ruleId has been the wrong default - reminder_due was the first - so the pattern is worth naming: a rule id that is not per-subject is the exception, not the norm. The old GPS-poll path is KEPT deliberately. It is the fallback for anyone on foreground-only location, and removing it here would make place reminders worse for them. So the flag stayed true while the app no longer HELD focus, every later turn short-circuited, and focus was never re-requested for the rest of the session. The fix is that the listener now clears `ducked` on LOSS, LOSS_TRANSIENT and LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK. Nothing else. It deliberately does not pause playback, alter capture, or grab focus back - taking focus from whatever just claimed it is how two apps fight over a car stereo. Losing focus is normal; never noticing was the bug. Worth recording why this was findable at all. That listener was added on 2026-08-17 as instrumentation, with a comment saying reacting before a real log pull "would be exactly the kind of guess this file's own delicacy warns against". location-intelligence 06location-intelligence 07location-intelligence 09

The caching research came back bigger than the question it was asked. STORAGE IS ZERO, not "until we check" Routing returns Cache-Control: no-cache with no max-age. Clause 11.4 permits caching only up to "the maximum age indicated in such cache control headers", and nothing is indicated - so the carve-out permits zero. "Results" covers a travel-time integer exactly as it covers a polyline; there is no derived-number allowance of the kind Google and HERE grant. On-device is not a loophole: 11.4.1 regulates caching "in clients" and the phone IS the client. Clause 11.6.1 independently forbids creating "any secondary or derived database" from Results, which is what a table of accumulated ETAs is. That is a second, independent reason decision 15 chose a global prep buffer - the history a learned buffer would need cannot legally exist. THE LICENCE QUESTION I DID NOT ASK The free key licenses "internal evaluation and testing by you", and the paid tier is scoped to apps with "Asset Management Functionality" licensed to end users. LEGION is neither. Kevin read the former as covering a sideloaded personal build with one developer and one user - recorded as decision 17, a deliberate reading of an ambiguous term rather than something missed. Stated with its uncertainty intact: the pricing page advertises the free tier without ever calling it Evaluation Use, and neither document maps the two onto each other. Failure mode is a revoked key, never a bill - there is no card. ATTRIBUTION DROPPED, against my recommendation Kevin's call, decision 19. I argued for keeping "per TomTom" because decision 6 exists so a third-party claim never sounds like LEGION's own. The cost is stated once on the map and not re-litigated. The counter-argument is real: 17.3 wants the Copyright API and a LOGO for Routing results, a voice surface cannot render one, so no spoken phrasing was ever compliant. Decision 19 NARROWS decision 6 rather than reversing it - NWS, USGS, NIFC, AirNow, FEMA and FBI results are still always attributed. Decision 4's row now points at its own supersessions instead of contradicting them. Also filed ticket 09 as KIV: the rest of the TomTom surface area. Kevin's key enables reverse geocoding, places search, traffic incidents, reachable range, snap-to-roads and more. Inventoried with a view on which are plausible for a voice assistant and which are not - and noting that TomTom's own Geofencing API is already decided against, because the Android OS one is free, on-device and needs no round trip. This repo already carries a standing warning from its own Android Auto research - "Never touch audio routing directly ... setCommunicationDevice and startBluetoothSco are forbidden once Telecom owns the call." That warning is about a call LEGION itself owns through its ConnectionService, which is a different situation from a cellular call owned by the system dialer. Close enough that assuming success would be the exact kind of guess this codebase keeps getting burned by, so CallAudioRoute asks and then checks what the route actually is, and names what it landed on instead when it did not move - a Bluetooth headset or the car legitimately winning is the likely case in Kevin's own use. The gap is stated rather than hidden: the readback is immediate, so a dialer that re-routes a second later is not caught. Cost is bounded - he hears the wrong speaker and says so - and polling audio state for seconds while he is trying to talk to someone is worse. A refused speaker does NOT make the answer a failure. The call is connected either way, and the two are reported as separate facts; success=false there would have the assistant say it could not answer a call it had just answered. Two tests pin that, including that a plain answer says nothing about the route at all. setCommunicationDevice on API 31+, the deprecated isSpeakerphoneOn below it. MODIFY_AUDIO_SETTINGS was already declared. 1809 tests green. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Three permissions, each verified against AOSP rather than assumed. WHY IT ONLY EVER SAID "A CALL" Not an oversight - the old code documented the limit and worked around it. TelephonyRegistry computes `r.canReadCallLog() ? phoneNumber : ""` on every callback delivery, so an app without READ_CALL_LOG is handed an EMPTY STRING, not null. LEGION held READ_PHONE_STATE only, so a generic line was the honest answer available. Now declared: READ_CALL_LOG (the only thing that delivers the number), READ_CONTACTS (number to name via PhoneLookup), ANSWER_PHONE_CALLS (an ordinary dangerous permission - TelecomServiceImpl checks it and its app-op and nothing else, so no dialer role is needed). READ_CALL_LOG is hard-restricted and would block a Play listing. LEGION is sideloaded and never listed, and adb install allowlists it by default. Written into the manifest so the day that changes, the constraint is already there. DO NOT migrate to TelephonyCallback.CallStateListener. Its onCallStateChanged has no number parameter at all - AOSP's dispatch comment says "The new callback does NOT provide the phone number" - so modernising off the deprecated PhoneStateListener would silently delete this feature. Said in the manifest and on the class. FOUR OUTCOMES, NONE OF THEM A GUESS CallerId resolves a contact name, a bare number, a genuinely withheld number, and "I am not allowed to look" - and keeps the last two apart. "I cannot see who is calling" and "the caller is unknown" are different claims, and collapsing them tells Kevin his caller withheld a number when the app was simply never permitted to check. Same shape as rendering a refused calendar permission as an empty day, which is settled decision 20. The announcement also stops offering what it cannot do: with no answer permission the prompt explicitly forbids offering to answer or decline. A BLOCKER FOUND BY TRACING, NOT BY TESTING isInCall was set true on RINGING, and LiveSessionController refuses to open a turn while isInCall - so the exact moment Kevin wants to say "answer it" was the moment the app showed "ON A CALL" and stopped listening. Voice answering was impossible before this and nothing would have reported that. Split into isRinging and isInCall: the proactive gate treats both as silence, the voice path deliberately does not. THE HONESTY PROBLEM acceptRingingCall() returns void. It reports nothing about whether the call was answered, so returning "probably fine" would push a lie one layer up into what the assistant says. CallActions instead WATCHES the phone's call state and reports what it observed: answering means RINGING became OFFHOOK. endCall does return a boolean and it is used, plus the same state check, because a true return is not the same as the ringing having stopped. That matters most for the case Android will not do at all: self-managed calls - WhatsApp, Signal, Teams - are silently ignored for a non-dialer app, with no error. The state check is what turns that silence into "that did not work, and here is why" instead of a confident false claim. Emergency calls cannot be ended either. Both named in the tool descriptions rather than discovered. Nine tests on the two describe() functions, which are the sentences that actually reach his ears. 1803 total, green. APK assembles, manifest merges. OWED on the phone: everything. Whether the number arrives, whether PhoneLookup matches his contacts, whether answering by voice beats the dialer UI to it, and whether the wake word can even be heard over a ringing phone - that last one is not addressed here and may well be the next problem. Ticket 08: `play_music`'s playlist type routed straight through public `/v1/search`, which is the wrong endpoint for "play my Roadtrip playlist" - search ranks the whole catalogue and its limit is capped at 10, so a hundred public playlists with similar names can bury the driver's own. SpotifyWebApi.myPlaylists() reads and caches `/me/playlists` (15-minute TTL, reasoning written into the code - long enough that a drive full of play/add requests costs at most one call, short enough that a freshly shared playlist shows up the same sitting). bestPlaylistMatch() fuzzy- matches the spoken name against that cache first (exact/containment/ Levenshtein tiers, all pure and unit-tested); only when nothing clears the threshold does resolvePlaylist() fall through to search, and play_music says so out loud when it does, naming what actually played. Each cached playlist carries a `readable` flag (owned by the account, or collaborative) per the research's hard boundary: `GET /playlists/{id}` only returns items for playlists the user owns or collaborates on, so a followed editorial playlist (Discover Weekly) is a real result the driver can still ask to play, but never one LEGION can write to. control_music gains `add_to_playlist` (POST /playlists/{id}/items - the /tracks -> /items migration the research called out), targeting the CURRENTLY PLAYING track, resolved through the library-only findMyPlaylist (never falls through to public search - adding to someone else's playlist was never what "add this to Roadtrip" meant). An unreadable match is named as unreadable before any write is attempted, never silently skipped and never reported as "no such playlist" - the exact case ticket 08 was filed to cover. No new tool declarations (ticket 03's one-net-new budget was already spent on get_music_queue): playlist-by-name folds into play_music's existing playlist type, and add_to_playlist folds into control_music's action enum alongside a new playlistName param. spotify-voice 02
66d1d4c · 4 files
Ticket 02 of the spotify-voice map. Implements the one play path every tool on this map funnels through (isInstalled -> ensureConnected -> ConnectApi.connectSwitchToLocalDevice() -> PlayerApi.play(uri)) instead of a bare play(uri) that assumed a device was already active. The switch-to-local step is what solves the cold case: asking for music with Spotify closed. App Remote's connect() alone creates an active device but doesn't say it's THIS phone; connectSwitchToLocalDevice() does, best-effort, before the play call lands. playUri now returns a SpotifyController.PlayOutcome instead of a bare Boolean, so a failed connect gets one of four distinct spoken lines (CouldNotFindSpotifyApp, NotLoggedInException, UserNotAuthorizedException, OfflineModeException) rather than one generic string, plus PlayRejected for a play() call that reached Spotify and was refused. The outcome -> message mapping and the connect-Throwable -> outcome mapping are both pure functions (SpotifyController.message/outcomeForConnectFailure), same shape as NavigationController's own outcome/message split, so they're covered by a plain-JVM test with no Context and no SDK connection. Also, per Kevin (2026-08-19): the foreground service now holds the App Remote connection itself (connectSilently in onCreate) instead of only ever connecting on the first voice command or from MainActivity.onResume. This deliberately violates Spotify's own documented guidance to connect in onStart and disconnect in onStop - the violation and the reason (latency on every utterance, in a car) are written into the code at both call sites so a future reader doesn't fix it back. Wires PlayerApi.subscribeToPlayerState() on every successful connect, exposed as SpotifyController.playerState (a StateFlow<PlayerState?>). Nothing reads it yet - tickets 07 and 09 do - and NowPlayingController's own reporting is deliberately unchanged in this ticket. Adds UserApi.getCapabilities().canPlayOnDemand as a best-effort, non-blocking check after a successful play: if it says the account can't play on demand, PlayOutcome.Started carries a spoken warning. Not a gate (this UX stays Premium-only by design) - it exists only so a non-Premium account is told in words instead of silently degraded. Does not touch SpotifyWebApi.kt's SCOPES list (owned by a parallel ticket on its own branch). Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Ticket 10 decides what it may MEAN before ticket 11 builds it, because the driver cannot tell a good recommendation from a hallucinated one by listening. Keep the conversation when the socket dies, and say so when we cannot
no ticket
0e3319b · 4 files
Kevin, on a real drive: "after a few turns, it doesnt remember the previous turn what we said. the context drops." Gemini Live keeps history in the SOCKET, so anything that ends a socket ends the memory. The app resisted none of it: GeminiLiveSession.kt carried the comment "goAway / sessionResumptionUpdate are ignored in this version" while buildSetup requested neither resumption nor compression. The server has been telling us it was about to cut, and handing us the handle that would have let us continue, and we threw both away. Now: - buildSetup requests sessionResumption, sending the stored handle when there is one, and contextWindowCompression with a sliding window. - sessionResumptionUpdate is captured; a resumable handle is kept ON THE CONTROLLER, which is the whole point - it must outlive the session object it came from. - goAway is parsed for its timeLeft and we close DELIBERATELY a margin early, so the cutoff is a planned handover rather than a surprise abort. "goAway" joins NORMAL_CLOSE_REASONS so our own planned close never flashes CONNECTION LOST at the driver. Compression addresses a DIFFERENT ender than a network drop - the window filling - and is commented as such so nobody later mistakes it for the fix. THE HONESTY HALF, which was the actual bug. A resume that works says nothing; continuity is the expected case. A thread that could NOT be resumed now flashes "RECONNECTED - LOST TRACK OF WHAT WE WERE SAYING" and opens the next turn by telling the MODEL it does not remember, instead of beginConversation(null) answering cold. An assistant that has forgotten and does not say so is asserting a continuity it does not have - the same rule that put a facts prohibition in AriaBrain earlier tonight. A crisis teardown clears the handle too: that conversation must never silently resume. Transcript replay was rejected. It is turn-boundary text, not continuable session state, and replaying it risks the model reading old text as new driver speech. My own brief justified skipping it on the grounds that companion text is not captured; the executing agent checked and CORRECTED me - subtitles = true is hardcoded now (:492, "a core UX surface, not debug-only"), so companion text IS stored. The conclusion stands on the better reason, not the stale one. Protocol fields were fetched from ai.google.dev/api/live and grepped, not recalled: sessionResumption.handle, sessionResumptionUpdate.newHandle/resumable, goAway.timeLeft, contextWindowCompression.slidingWindow. UNPROVEN, and neither is small: no real goAway timeLeft has ever been observed, so the 3s margin is a guess with a comment saying so; and the protocol gives no ack for a rejected or expired handle, so "handle present means resume worked" is the best signal available, not a confirmation. Reproduce without a car: adb shell cmd connectivity airplane-mode enable, wait for the socket to die mid-conversation, disable, then tap. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

On-device, from the Android Auto rig: asked about his day, LEGION told Kevin he had "a dentist appointment at 3". There is no dentist row anywhere in his real database - zero matches across every text column of every table. It was invented whole. The prompt had a rule for ACTIONS ("Always call the matching tool before claiming you've done something") and a rule for MEMORY ("don't claim to remember something without checking first") and NO RULE FOR FACTS. Nothing anywhere said that a statement about the driver's own record has to come from a tool call. So the question a companion gets asked most - what's on today - was the one question with no honesty rule attached to it. Same shape as the navigation lie in drive-test 03: the general principle exists but only binds where a worked example points it. There the missing case was a capability that did not exist; here it is a fact nobody looked up. Now stated as a hard prohibition covering appointments, reminders, tasks, figures, dates, car details, meals and spend: call the tool first, and if it returns nothing say there is nothing, because an empty day is a real answer. An invented appointment is worse than "I don't have anything" - the driver cannot tell them apart, and one of them can make him miss something real. A prompt rule is a mitigation, not a guarantee. drive-test 04 owns the question of whether this needs a structural guard rather than words, and how a regression would ever be caught - this one was caught by a human on a head unit, which does not scale. A conversation waits for the driver, not for a ten-second timer
no ticket
1e3ee04 · 1 file
Field report, real drive 2026-08-18: "conversation drops after 3 turns." After every completed turn the vadMode branch armed a 10s idle timer. On expiry, keepWarm && vadMode took parkWarm(): mic stopped, socket parked, LiveEvent.Idle emitted, and LiveSessionController's Idle branch set Phase.IDLE with NO showNotice - unlike the Closed branch right below it, which does flash one. So a normal driving pause (mirror check, a merge, finishing a thought) silently ended hands-free listening and put the strip back to "Tap to talk". Three exchanges is about how long it takes to accumulate one 10s gap. This exact failure had already been found once, during onboarding, and fixed by making the timeout a per-start parameter - see idleTimeoutMs's own comment, which says the 10s default "was being hit by completely normal 'let me think about that' pauses". No caller ever passed the parameter, so every conversation still ran on 10 seconds, on a drive, where such pauses are more frequent rather than less. Kevin's call, asked directly: a conversation now waits INDEFINITELY. It ends when he ends it (tapping the strip - onTap's `inConversation -> stop()`), when the socket dies (which already flashes CONNECTION LOST and returns the strip to a persistent "Tap to talk"), or on the crisis path. Any timer left armed by an earlier turn is cancelled so a stale one cannot fire mid-chat. armIdleTimeout now governs speak-only sessions only, which is its one remaining caller: vadMode false, no mic open, nothing to keep warm for. The warm park itself is unaffected and still reached by the proactive suppressMicNextTurn branch. Deliberately NOT addressed here: the separate context-loss defect. Gemini Live keeps history in the socket, goAway is ignored (GeminiLiveSession.kt:772) and no contextWindowCompression or resumption handle is requested, so a socket death still cold-restarts with no memory. Ticketed, not fixed. Known consequence, accepted: an active conversation no longer has any upper bound, so a forgotten one keeps a live mic and a billed session open until the service is torn down. Onboarding-complete must mean the driver saved a key, not that one exists
no ticket
d7cdd82 · 2 files
Two tests were red on this branch. They were not the same kind of problem. ProactiveBusTest > blocked while onboarding is incomplete was a REAL DEFECT. OnboardingState.isComplete delegated to GeminiKeyProvider.hasKey(), which deliberately falls back to BuildConfig.GEMINI_API_KEY so a convenience dev build does not need a key re-entered by hand. That fallback is correct for "what key do we call Gemini with" and wrong for "did the driver finish setup". On any local build with a real key in local.properties the gate silently stopped gating: clearing the on-file key still left onboarding reading complete, so ProactiveBus.speakIfAllowed no longer blocked. A distributed build ships -Pnokey and an empty field, so the two checks already agreed there - only the dev build diverged, which is why this hid. isComplete now reads CompanionProfile.geminiKey directly. GeminiKeyProvider is unchanged; the fallback still serves the call sites that need a usable key. Consequence on a dev build with a baked-in key: no prewarm and no proactive speech until a key is saved once through ui/KeyScreen.kt. BioDigestBuilderTest > bodyweight reports a weekly average was the TEST's fault - a fixture anchored 2 days back crosses the Monday boundary when the suite runs on a Monday or Tuesday, so the second reading fell into the previous week and the average came out 180.0 instead of 181.0. Anchored to weekStartEpoch(now) instead. `now` itself stays wall-clock because BioDigestBuilder anchors "today"/"this week" the same way; pinning it broke two other tests in the file. Full suite green, 1555 tests, verified with --rerun rather than a cached up-to-date result. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Android hands a losing capture ZEROES with no exception, no callback and no AudioRecord state change. GeminiLiveSession has detected that since ticket 15 wave 2, but isSilenced had exactly one production consumer - a mirror into CarProbeLog - so the one state where LEGION cannot hear was the one state it never said out loud. It kept drawing "Listening...". CompanionPhase.silenced carries the signal process-wide. A StateFlow and not notice: silencing is an ONGOING condition, and a four-second flash would clear while LEGION was still deaf. Two guards on the mirror, both against a dead session outliving its socket: an identity check so a torn-down session's late emit cannot stomp the live one, and a clear in session's own property setter so a stale true cannot survive any of the ten sites that drop a session. Render-only: nothing stored was ever incorrect. Five regression tests, built the way the WRITE path builds it (UTC midnight) rather than the way the older fixtures did (device-zone midnight). That mismatch is exactly why the existing tests could not have caught this - their fixture and the code under test shared one convention by construction. Stop an ask_<domain> loop from claiming a write that never ran
no ticket
f97e1d8 · 4 files
Measured on-device: a driver spoke workout sets during a real 21:42-21:45 voice session. workout_set_logs has no row from that night, yet the app told him it was recorded. Logcat for the window proves log_workout_set was never dispatched at all - the driver's request went into ask_goals, whose investigate loop called only list_goals/ask_advisor (read tools) and still answered with prose the old code spoke verbatim as success = true. Root cause, traced two layers deep: - SubAgent.kt's investigate loop returned AgentResult.Success for ANY round that came back with zero functionCalls, with no memory of what actually ran - a sub-agent's prose alone could claim an action happened. - LiveToolbox.agentResult mapped every AgentResult.Success straight to result(true, ...), so that unchecked prose reached the driver as fact. - Compounding: the forced-answer round set functionCallingConfig.mode = "NONE", so a loop that had spent its whole budget on reads was physically unable to call a write tool even if it tried on its last round. What changed: 1. SubAgent.investigate gains mutatingToolNames: Set<String> = emptySet() (default keeps every existing caller byte-identical). The loop tracks, in its own local state - never MidnightEvents - which of those names actually got dispatched, and returns them as AgentResult.Success.mutatingToolsCalled: List<String> (also defaulted, so ask/askTyped/askWithUsage are unaffected). 2. LiveToolbox.MUTATING_TOOLS: an explicit, named set of every dispatch() branch that writes to Room or actuates real hardware (log_*/set_*/ create_*/manage_*/clear_pending_transaction/undo_last_log/tag_place/ forget_place/register_vehicle/remember/accept_proposal/activate_garage/ categorize_transactions/close_goal), enumerated from the real branches rather than inferred from a prefix at call time - deliberately excludes the five ask_<domain> dispatchers themselves (a router isn't a write) and the three UI-scoped hand-offs (dispatch() writes nothing for them). mutatingToolsFor(domain) intersects this with DISPATCHED[domain], so each ask_<domain> call passes investigate() only the mutating names actually reachable in that domain's own tool set. 3. LiveToolbox.agentResult gains requireMutation: Boolean = false and routes AgentResult.Success through the new pure successOrMutationRefusal (extracted the same way LiveSessionController.shouldRestoreAfterToolCall was, for unit coverage with no network/Room/Robolectric): when requireMutation is true and mutatingToolsCalled is empty, the sub-agent's text is discarded entirely and a plain "not recorded" refusal is spoken instead - never the false "logged it" that caused this. 4. The forced-answer trap: functionCallingConfig.mode = "NONE" now only fires on round maxModelCalls + 1, not maxModelCalls. Tools stay enabled through the old cutoff round (still nudged to wrap up, same timing as before), so a write that's still outstanding gets one more real chance to run; only a model that's STILL not done after that hits the true, tool-free backstop. Costs at most one extra POST, only when needed. What this does NOT fix, and why - the honest gap: requireMutation stays false at all five ask_<domain> call sites and everywhere else in this file. dispatch() only ever sees args.optString("question") for these calls - free prose - and there is no reliable, non-guessing way to tell "log my three sets of squats" (a write) from "what did I lift last week" (a read) from that string alone; both are legitimate questions the same dispatcher answers. Flipping this on blindly for a mixed domain (fleet/body/pantry) would refuse real reads; flipping it on for a domain with zero mutating tools in its own list (goals/mail) would refuse every call, including the reads that are its entire job. Per the brief's own constraint, this stops at making the mechanism real, tested, and available for a future caller that CAN tell (e.g. a dispatcher schema extended with an explicit intent argument the model itself declares, the way accept_proposal already requires an explicit id rather than trusting prose) - not at guessing. New: LiveToolboxMutationGateTest covers the three cases the brief asked for directly against successOrMutationRefusal - write-shaped + a mutating call (success), write-shaped + none (refusal, sub-agent prose discarded), read-shaped + none (success, never refused). Review of the seven-commit mic-robustness pass came back four SHIP, three findings. All three close here as one correction pass. 1. MUST-FIX (b62a204's retry branch): the short-capture retry set capturing = true and continued without discarding the model's own bogus reply first. That reply was still queued on audioQueue / on the AudioTrack, so the reopened mic captured Zero's own voice - the exact half-duplex violation micLoop's own mic-open comment warns about - and could re-trigger the same false-VAD pattern with the turn's one retry already spent. Now calls flushAudio() and resets speakingThisTurn = false before capturing = true, mirroring the barge-in path in beginConversation(). flushAudio()'s turnGeneration bump (ab42e8a) is correct here too: the bogus reply's remaining chunks should stale out the same way a driver's barge-in tap stales them. 2. SHOULD-FIX (ab42e8a): turnGeneration was a @Volatile Int bumped with `++`, which is read-modify-write, not atomic. flushAudio() has genuinely concurrent callers - the OkHttp socket-callback thread (handleServerContent's interrupted/crisis branches) and the mic coroutine (beginConversation's barge-in path, and now micLoop's own retry branch above) - so a lost increment could land the counter back on a value a stale snapshotted message still holds, resurrecting the exact race the counter exists to close. Replaced with java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger: incrementAndGet() in flushAudio(), get() at the snapshot and per-chunk comparison sites in handleServerContent. Comments updated to describe the new mechanism rather than the old one. 3. NIT (c0676d9 / 1938a87): the ERROR_DEAD_OBJECT recreation path stopped and released the dying record without emitting MicClosed, so the rebuilt record's fresh MicOpened had no matching close - unbalanced for any future consumer, and inconsistent with commit 1938a87's own claim that every stop emits. Now emits MicClosed ("AudioRecord dead, recreating") before tearing the old record down, and recording is cleared at that same point so the loop's finally block does not also emit a redundant close if recreation then fails and the session closes. Verification: compileDebugKotlin -Pnokey green. testDebugUnitTest: 1485 tests, 2 failed - both BioDigestBuilderTest, matching the pre-existing baseline from the prior commit exactly, unrelated to any file touched here. An AudioRecord read error is not "no data yet"
no ticket
1938a87 · 1 file
record.read(buffer, 0, buffer.size) returns a negative AudioRecord.ERROR_* constant on failure, not a byte count. ERROR_INVALID_OPERATION (-3), ERROR_BAD_VALUE (-2), ERROR_DEAD_OBJECT (-6), and plain ERROR (-1) were indistinguishable here from "n == 0, no data arrived yet" via `if (n <= 0) continue`, and unlike the `!capturing` idle branch just above (which delays 20ms), this path had no delay at all - a dead AudioRecord would busy-loop the mic coroutine silently forever, burning a core with no log line and no user-visible signal. Split n < 0 from n == 0. On any negative code: log the specific AudioRecord.ERROR_* name with TAG, breadcrumb it to CarProbeLog, and back off RECORD_READ_ERROR_BACKOFF_MS (20ms, matching the existing idle-branch delay - the point is only that some delay exists) before retrying. On ERROR_DEAD_OBJECT specifically: tear the AudioRecord and its attached effects down and rebuild both from the same recordBuilder config, once per session (recreatedRecordOnce, distinct in scope from the per-turn retriedThisTurn above - a dead AudioRecord is a hardware/ driver failure, not a VAD hiccup, and micLoop itself only runs once per session). record and effects are now var for exactly this reason; the recordingCallback closure registered earlier already reads both dynamically off the current value at callback time, so no separate re-registration was needed for it. If the rebuilt AudioRecord also fails to initialize, the session closes with "microphone unavailable" (the same message the initial creation failure already used) rather than looping. Not unit-testable: this is control flow around a live AudioRecord inside a suspend loop, same reachability shape as the other micLoop changes in this session - there is no plain-JVM seam to extract the decision from without touching android.media directly, which throws "not mocked" under gradlew testDebugUnitTest per this repo's own Testing/singletons/composables playbook note. Phase.LISTENING was set from the socket's TurnComplete event, which fires before capture is physically live - the real AudioRecord.startRecording() sits behind awaitPlaybackDrained() (up to PLAYBACK_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS 1500ms + MIC_REOPEN_SETTLE_MS 60ms), and openMicForUser() itself hasn't even run yet at the point TurnComplete is emitted. So the UI claimed Listening for up to ~1.56s while the mic was still shut, and kept claiming it if capture then silently died. Same defect class as 083a6a6's Phase.THINKING fix (L30): a phase claiming one thing while the code does another. Add LiveEvent.MicOpened/MicClosed, emitted at the actual AudioRecord.startRecording()/stop() call sites in micLoop - not the capturing=true/false intent flips (those already log to MidnightEvents.micState and are left alone). MicOpened fires right after startRecording() returns, MicClosed fires at every place the mic is actually stopped: the ordinary half-duplex-mute close, the short-capture-retry give-up path (commit above), and a session teardown/exception that leaves capture running with no other exit. The retry-reopen path deliberately does NOT emit either - the record never physically stops there, so there is nothing to signal. LiveSessionController's TurnComplete handler no longer sets Phase.LISTENING for the conversationMode branch (the segment still stays open - this is still active talk time); MicOpened now owns that transition, not gated on conversationMode so it also fixes a second existing gap where a bare tap-to-listen (beginConversation with no opener) left the phase stuck on the Connected branch's Phase.THINKING("...") forever, since nothing previously moved it. MicClosed is exposed but not consumed for a phase change yet - SpeakingStarted already covers the ordinary mute case at effectively the same moment, and a teardown close is immediately followed by its own Idle/Closed event. Not unit-testable: LiveEvent dispatch, AudioRecord lifecycle, and Phase are all only exercised end-to-end through a live socket and LiveSessionController's own coroutine scope. A naive restore lets the FIRST one to finish drop the UI out of THINKING while siblings are still running. Fixed with a refcount (activeToolCalls): only the transition to zero restores. scope is CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Main.immediate + ...), confined to a single thread, so a plain Int is correct - no AtomicInteger needed. 2. Something else may have already moved the phase since the tool started - the model started speaking (SpeakingStarted -> SPEAKING) or the socket closed (Closed/Idle -> IDLE) mid-tool. Restoring unconditionally would stomp that. Fixed by only restoring when the phase is STILL THINKING at the moment the last tool call finishes. Both checks live in the new shouldRestoreAfterToolCall(remainingActiveToolCalls, currentPhase), on the companion object (not an instance member) so it needs no live Context/GeminiLiveSession/Room to call - LiveSessionController itself can't be constructed from a plain JVM test (same constraint GeminiLiveSessionEpisodicExclusionTest already documents for a sibling class). Make SubAgent's HTTP round-trip actually cancellable
no ticket
854406f · 1 file
postOnce was a plain (non-suspend) HttpURLConnection call invoked from the suspend postRaw. Coroutine cancellation is cooperative, and a thread blocked inside Java socket I/O has no cooperation point to check - it only notices cancellation once the read returns on its own. That made every timeout above it inert: AgentTool.timeoutMs wrapping tool.run, investigate's own budgetMs, and LiveSessionController.handleToolCall's 45s withTimeoutOrNull for SUB_AGENT_TOOLS. The real ceiling was connectTimeout 15s / readTimeout 30s per attempt, times postRaw's one retry - enough for "log a bunch of meals" (routed through ask_body -> SubAgent.investigate as of 2a1c18e) to leave the UI on "Listening..." for minutes while a cancelled call kept running anyway. postOnce is now `private suspend fun postOnce(...) = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { ... }`. Two things make cancellation real rather than cosmetic: 1. withContext(Dispatchers.IO) makes this suspend point itself cancellable. When the surrounding job is cancelled, withContext rethrows CancellationException at ITS OWN boundary as the call unwinds - not inside the block, so the block's `catch (e: Exception)` (which CancellationException is technically a subtype of) never gets a chance to swallow it. Traced: postRaw's retry loop only re-enters ("attempt == 0" -> delay -> continue) if postOnce RETURNS a value; on cancellation postOnce never returns to postRaw at all, it propagates the cancellation through the suspend call, so the loop cannot retry a cancelled attempt. No extra isActive guard needed - this is withContext's own contract, not an assumption. 2. `coroutineContext.job.invokeOnCompletion` registers a callback that calls connection.disconnect() the moment this coroutine's job completes for any non-null cause (i.e. cancellation). That's what actually unblocks the thread parked in outputStream/responseCode/ inputStream - without it, withContext's own cancellation check only fires when the blocking call eventually returns on its own, i.e. never before the socket's own 30s read timeout. The handle is disposed in the existing finally alongside connection.disconnect(), so a normal completion cleans it up as a no-op and a cancelled one as a fired one - either order is harmless. connectTimeout/readTimeout values are untouched; they remain the backstop for a stall under no caller timeout at all, not the thing actually bounding a stuck call anymore. Traced: grepped all callers of postOnce/postRaw inside SubAgent.kt - postRaw has exactly four callers (ask, askWithUsage, askTyped, runInvestigation), all already suspend funs; postOnce has exactly one caller (postRaw). No non-coroutine entry point exists that this change could break. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

The app targets SDK 34, not 36 - the A25 runs Android 16, which is a different thing entirely - so the six-hour dataSync cap, the BOOT_COMPLETED foreground-service block and the global DND lockout are all dormant today and armed only by a targetSdk bump that sideloading means nothing forces. And I cited MEMORY as establishing Samsung OEM aggression on this phone; the file actually attributes that adb failure to Git Bash path mangling and has no pm clear entry at all. The research rebuilt that section on Samsung's own documentation instead of my misreading. The threat turns out not to be the cap I sent it looking for. Samsung's own sleeping-apps layer puts an app unused for around three days into a restricted bucket - one alarm per day, no network - while the foreground service keeps running and everything looks healthy. A voice assistant used daily without its UI ever being opened is precisely that profile, which is what LEGION is. Also found: on Android 16, applying already at target 34, jobs running concurrently with a foreground service now obey the runtime quota, so the service no longer buys unlimited WorkManager time. AriaForegroundService uses dataSync as its base type because it is the only type with no runtime prerequisite, and it is the only one with a kill timer; neither it nor LedgerIngestService implements onTimeout, so the eventual failure is a fatal RemoteServiceException rather than degradation. And no app-only DND bypass exists at any importance or category, which bounds what may ever speak during quiet hours. Recommendations are recorded but not acted on: dropping dataSync changes foreground service behaviour and is a decision for the delivery ticket, not something to do unattended at night. Ten items need the phone, and they have one gate: whether the service survives a twelve-hour screen-off unplugged run at all. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Stop the import rekey duplicating a car, without the hang this time
import-sync-duplication 01
35c4929 · 3 files
The bug was never fixed, only latched around: rekeyExistingRows still blind UPDATEd a row into a duplicate when the destination identity already existed, and what stopped it on Kevin's phone was completed_v3 latching after 17 colliding rows were deleted by hand. Any device that has not latched still carries it, the retired A17k included. The first attempt at this hung on the device and was reverted to a stash. The ticket blamed concurrent sync-writer contention. The likelier cause is duller: obd_samples has no index at all beyond its primary key, and that attempt still issued one UPDATE or DELETE per bundle row - up to 11,511 - each with a WHERE over pid, timestamp and vehicleId. That is eleven thousand full table scans over a table holding up to 36,694 rows, on a table this very bug inflates. It fits the symptom without needing contention to explain it. So the apply step is now set-based: bucket candidates in memory against the identity set already loaded once, then one DELETE and one UPDATE per table per move, matched against a temp table. Worst case becomes a few scans of the table rather than one scan per row. A source row is deleted only when its full identity already exists at the destination, which is what makes deletion safe rather than lossy, and the identity columns are named per table on the ticket. Four repeated passes converge to one row. The honest limit: this cannot run on Kevin's phone at all, because his import is latched complete. Exercising it needs a device with completed_v3 unset, a colliding bundle present, and enough obd_samples volume to reproduce the timing. Ticket 01 of the drive-ui map, resolved the day it was charted. Findings carry per-claim source-type labels and seven explicit not-established flags. Multi-PID batching is CAN-only, settled twice independently: ISO 15031-5 defines the optional PID#2-#6 request rows only in its CAN clause and not in the ISO 9141-2 clause, and the ELM327 datasheet says the same in prose. One PID per round trip is a hard ceiling on a 1998 XJ, so "add one more reading" is a cadence decision rather than a layout one. The protocol floor is about 119ms per PID and 150-250ms is realistic, putting a three-PID set at roughly 1.3-2.2 Hz today and 2.4-2.7 after tuning. One genuine unused lever exists, the ELM327 responses digit, which is not CAN-only and which LEGION never sends. The headline is MAF. The Jeep 4.0L is speed-density with no MAF sensor and the standard conditions PID 0110 on the vehicle having one, so instantaneous mpg is very probably impossible on this car. Trip content now has to argue from average over known distance instead, and the fog entry is struck pending ticket 02 confirming 0110 is actually silent. The consequence that governs the rest of the map: a live gauge here steps about twice a second, so any UI implying smooth continuous motion is lying about the bus. That turns the motion question from taste into honesty, since a needle easing between two real readings invents every value in between. It is the estimates rule arriving somewhere nobody had pointed it before. Filed to the library in the same commit, per the tracker convention, and by hand rather than through the librarian. It can be neutered through the same channel that spread it: set newVehicleId = vehicleId and bump updatedAt, so LWW carries the harmless version to Drive and it wins. DriveReassigner.plan drops self-moves by design, so a neutered rule plans to nothing on every device forever. That property, written for another reason, is what allowed a clean exit. The sentinel re-key was repaired with a local UPDATE that sync could not see. obd_samples syncs UNION on an identity that includes vehicleId, so the originals stayed on Drive under the old id, came back on the next pull, and the next re-key made them look new again. The fix invents nothing. VehicleController.reassignDrive already writes a DriveReassignment rule for exactly this reason, and its doc comment from 2026-07-16 describes the failure mode almost word for word - a plain UPDATE "would leave the originals on Drive under the old id, and the next sync would re-insert them, cloning the drive onto both cars instead of moving it, permanently, on every device". The import then did that plain UPDATE. It now writes the rule instead. What makes a rule converge is where SyncEngine applies it: after the merge and before the snapshot it uploads is re-read, so Drive receives the corrected id rather than handing the old one back. The syncId is deterministic rather than a fresh UUID, because the import re-runs until its gate latches and six identical rules would each be replayed on every sync forever. The range is unbounded because a whole car's history is on the wrong id. Self-moves are never written, since the planner drops them as infinite no-ops. Five tests, 1334 -> 1339. No schema change. Dormant on Kevin's phone by design, and verified so: drive_reassignments holds 0 rows because the gate is latched and run() returns first. The code protects any device that still has an import to do; stage 1's outcome already protects this one. Not done unasked: writing the rule by hand to converge Drive here. That corrects this ticket's first draft, which reasoned that rekeyed rows were piling up. The rekey is not the duplicator; it is what makes each pulled batch invisible to the next pull, by moving it off the identity sync matches on. Both halves are needed to grow anything. Verified without running a sync. That mattered: a manual sync would have pushed the local duplicates to the shared Drive file and on to the other phone, which is the one thing worth not doing while diagnosing.
