Found while verifying the v19 to v20 migration against a copy of the real database. The migration was clean; a PRAGMA table_info comparison of all 44 entities against the generated schema flagged this as the only genuine difference. ledger_transactions.categoryPending is declared on the entity with no default, but the migration adds it with DEFAULT 0 - which SQLite requires when adding a NOT NULL column to a table with rows. Nobody added the matching @ColumnInfo. So a fresh install and a migrated install create that column with different DDL, permanently, which is the opposite of what section 5 asks for and what seven other columns in this codebase already do correctly. An audit of every default across all 44 entities found exactly one drifted column, so the problem is contained and the ticket is the whole of it. It has not bitten anything because Room treats an expected null default as "don't care" rather than "must have none", which is why the app opens at v19 today. That is a reason it is low priority, not a reason it is fine. The ticket warns against the tempting wrong fix: do not drop DEFAULT 0 from the historical migration. A migration must keep producing exactly what it always produced. The entity is what changes. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

The VIN decode now writes the car's identity back, instead of discarding it
fleet-maintenance 12
7ade299 · 9 files
refreshFromVin called decodeSpecs(vin), wrote sixteen spec fields, and threw away decode(vin)'s year/make/model/trim - parsed from the same vPIC response. Kevin's vehicle_specs has held a fully decoded Jeep VIN since 2026-07-26 while the vehicles row for the same id reads make='', model='', year=0. That blank identity is why screens say THIS CAR and why fetchRecalls returns empty. decodeAll makes one HTTP call and parses both halves. refreshFromVin applies the identity after saving specs. reconcileIdentityFromStoredVin re-decodes the VIN already on disk, so a repair needs the network but not the adapter. Policy is fill-blanks, never overwrite, straight out of VinDecoder's own class doc: a decode is a confirmable suggestion, not a silent overwrite of what the driver typed. A conflict on any one field aborts the whole write, and the reason is not tidiness - a disagreement is evidence the decode may not describe this car at all. A misread VIN, a transposed character, a dongle moved to another vehicle all present as one field not matching. Filling the blank fields from a decode you have reason to distrust writes another vehicle's facts into the row, where they then read as this car's own. Deliberately not setIdentity, which stamps confirmed = 1. That is right when the driver states the identity and wrong for a lookup filling in blanks on their behalf, so this path gets its own query and never claims that consent. Two review findings fixed before commit. READ VIN performed the write-back and discarded the outcome, so a refused write was invisible on that path while the other button said everything in words - the same defect this map exists to close, and it does not stop being one because the button had another job. And the conflict comparison now trims both sides: the decoder trims and title-cases, correctVehicle stores driver-typed text untouched, so a trailing space read as a real disagreement and aborted the write. A third finding is a decision, not a fix, and is filed on ticket 12: the voice recall tool gates on confirmed and the proactive startup push does not. That split was inert while decode-only cars had blank make and model. This change makes it reachable, so the same car can now have recalls announced at startup and refused when asked. 1121 tests, 0 failures. Room still v19, no schemas diff. Not yet on device. I asserted twice, in the map and on two tickets, that check_recalls sends an NHTSA query with empty make, empty model and model year 0. That was wrong, and I stated it before reading VinDecoder. fetchRecalls guards at its own entry and returns an empty list when year, make or model are missing. No request is made at all. The consequence is unchanged, which is why ticket 12 stays blocked: an empty list is indistinguishable from "this car has no open recalls." The app would report a clean bill of health on a car it never asked about. The guard ticket 12 needs is therefore not inside fetchRecalls, which already has one and is silent about it. It is at the button: year, make and model must be present before the check is offered, and their absence has to be said in words rather than rendering as a clean result. Kevin handed over an actual Bank of America statement today. Run through StatementDispatcher under Robolectric, it quarantined - and CLAUDE.md section 4 makes quarantine all-or-nothing, so his statement imported as ZERO rows. This is the primary deterministic path, the reason the LLM is only a fallback, and it had never once been given a real document. Two independent bugs, each fatal on its own. Multi-line rows. Real wires wrap their description over three lines and print the amount alone on a fourth. The parser assumed one transaction per line and threw "transaction row missing an amount" on the first wire. parseSectionBody now accumulates continuation lines until a money token appears, bounded at six so a genuinely amount-less row still fails fast instead of swallowing the section. Four of his sixteen transactions are wires. Section detection. Every section name appears TWICE on a real statement - once in the summary block near the top, once as the real transaction-table header. extractSection used indexOfFirst and locked onto the summary every time. The Deposits section only APPEARED to work: it started at the summary line and happened to span the right rows, so the accident looked like success. The ATM section then swallowed every deposit row, which surfaced as "expected a negative amount... Zelle payment". The reliable signal is that a real header is immediately followed by a Date column header; a summary occurrence is not. A section's body can also arrive in several pieces - Other subtractions appeared three times, its header reprinted after a page break - so the pieces are stitched before the total is checked once. And the page-furniture filter was anchored to a bare account line, while the real reprinted header carries a name before the account number and a date range after it; it is a substring test now. WHY 151 PASSING TESTS DID NOT CATCH EITHER: the fixtures and the parser were written from the same assumptions. A synthetic BofA statement authored by someone who believes rows are single-line contains only single-line rows, and its tests then confirm the belief rather than test it. Review cannot see this; there is nothing in the diff to notice. It is only visible against a document nobody on this side wrote. So the fixtures now imitate reality rather than our model of it: a summary block repeating all four section names with totals, a section split across a page break with its header and Date row reprinted, an account/name/date-range line and a Page N of M footer interleaved mid-section, alongside the multi-line wire and ordinary single-line rows. Every total derived programmatically from the row data. All invented names, ids and amounts - nothing from his statement, which was copied in, run, and deleted for each of the three attempts and is not in this repo. Verified on the real statement: 16 transactions, all 16 date-led rows accounted for, opening 366.44 plus net -310.94 lands exactly on the 55.50 ending balance the statement itself prints. 152 unit tests, 0 failures. NOT verified: the credit-card statement layout, which Kevin also has and which is a different format again. On today's evidence I would not assume it parses. BofA's CSV export prints no account number anywhere - confirmed on Kevin's real file, where every long digit run turns out to be a confirmation number or ACH id inside a description. accountId is what balances group on, what dedup keys on and what latestBalanceCents reads, so a CSV with a placeholder account would sit in a phantom account separate from the PDFs for the same physical account. With a checking account and a credit card both in play, guessing is not available. Kevin's ruling: the containing Drive subfolder names the account for any file that does not state one. <connected folder>/ checking/ stmt.csv, eStmt_2026-07-08.pdf credit/ stmt.csv, eStmt_2026-07-15.pdf listChildren now descends one level and tags each file with its containing folder. It also stops staging directories as if they were files - that was a pre-existing bug, not a new one: a subfolder came back as a child, failed to parse and landed UNREADABLE. Files directly in the connected root still work exactly as before. The mapping is keyed on the folder's SAF document id rather than its name, so renaming a folder cannot silently orphan it and start quarantining everything inside. Seeded from Application.onCreate per L12. No Room change - it is SharedPreferences. Two rules decide what happens when sources disagree, and both refuse to guess. A PDF's own printed account ALWAYS beats the folder mapping; the folder only fills a gap. And a PDF whose printed account CONTRADICTS its folder quarantines naming both values, because that means the file is in the wrong subfolder and silently trusting either side moves money into the wrong account. A file with no stated account in a folder with no mapping quarantines too, telling the user to map the folder - not a placeholder, not a default. CSV acceptance is gated on extension rather than mime, because SAF providers report CSVs as text/csv, application/vnd.ms-excel or application/octet-stream depending on the provider. PDFs stay mime-gated as before, and everything else still lands UNREADABLE rather than being fed to the LLM. That widening introduced a hazard the agent caught and I had not specified: a .csv that is NOT BofA's layout now passes the acceptance gate, and the PDF parsers call PDDocument.load(), which throws a raw IOException on non-PDF bytes that the catch chain never handled. A %PDF magic-byte guard now stands in front of every PdfBox call, with a test pinning it. The ledger screen gains a folder-to-account section: discovered subfolders, each with a one-tap chip from known accounts, a free-text entry for a new one, and clear. 149 unit tests, 0 failures. NOT verified, and it is the part that matters: no device today. The SAF recursion query itself has never run - directory detection, how a real Drive provider reports subfolder mime types, and whether CSV extensions survive the round trip are all reasoned from the existing working root-level query, not exercised. That is exactly the class of thing that has only ever proved out on hardware in this project. The mapping UI compiles and has previews but has not been rendered. A deterministic parser for BofA's mid-cycle CSV export
no ticket
2d188e7 · 5 files
Statements only exist as PDFs at month end, so mid-month the ledger goes stale. BofA exports posted activity as CSV any time, and that export is born-digital and structured - so this is a DETERMINISTIC path. No LLM, no spend gate, no billed call. Mid-month updates become free and exact, which is a better answer than pasting a transaction list into a chat box and asking a model to re-emit numbers it just read. The export is also a BETTER anchor than the PDFs are. It states a beginning balance, total credits, total debits, an ending balance, AND a running balance per row. That is three independent reconciliation checks where the PDF parsers get one, and the parser uses all three, each with its own userMessage naming the actual figures - which check failed is the useful information. Verified against Kevin's real export before writing a line: all three anchors hold to the cent (-6.31 + 6352.91 = 6346.60; credits 6460.05; debits -107.14; running balance continuous across all 12 rows). The fixtures in this commit are SYNTHETIC and mirror that shape - his real statement is not in the repo. The first transaction row repeats the beginning balance with an empty Amount. It seeds the running-balance anchor and is never emitted as a transaction. Dispatcher order is load-bearing, not stylistic. The CSV parser runs FIRST because its recognition is pure text matching and falls through cleanly on PDF bytes, while the reverse is unsafe: the PDF parsers call PDDocument.load(), which throws a raw IOException on CSV bytes that the existing catch chain does not handle. A test pins exactly that hazard. 135 unit tests, 0 failures. TWO THINGS THIS DOES NOT DO, both surfaced rather than half-wired: IngestPipeline.stage hard-rejects any mimeType that is not application/pdf, and LedgerController hardcodes that same type, so a CSV is marked UNREADABLE before the dispatcher ever sees it. Nothing here changes that. And the export contains NO ACCOUNT NUMBER - confirmed on the real file, not assumed; every long digit run in it is a confirmation number or ACH id inside a description. accountId is what balances group on, what dedup keys on and what latestBalanceCents reads, so CSV rows currently carry a placeholder and would sit in a phantom account separate from the PDF rows for the same physical account. With both a checking account and a credit card in play, guessing is not available. Kevin's ruling: per-account Drive subfolders, with the containing folder naming the account for any file that does not state one. That needs scanner recursion (listChildren is flat today and does not even skip directories) and a folder-to-account mapping, which is its own commit. JSONObject.isNull treats an absent key and an explicit null identically, so a row with no syncId maps to identity [null] - and two such rows collide as the same row. Harmless today because backfillSyncIds runs before every pass, but SyncMerge.plan itself has no defence if a future caller skips that step. A missing or null clock reads as 0L through optLong's default. Two rows both missing a clock give 0 > 0 = false: silently inert rather than erroring or letting remote win. A real shape for ingested_files.lastAttemptAt before a first attempt. Equal clocks favour the local row, because the comparison is strict. A remote row written at the same clock with different content is dropped exactly like a stale one. 130 unit tests, 0 failures. 6c1bfb0 · 15 files
Kevin's call, 2026-08-02: two people, two phones, one Google account. He wants an Alfred-style assistant, his wife wants a different one. So identity stops being a single global thing and becomes a SET of named profiles that sync, with each device choosing which one is active locally. This does not reopen CLAUDE.md section 1. That ruling killed PER-CAR identity - cars are data, not identities - and said nothing about per-PERSON configurability, which is what this is. Profiles live in a new Room table and sync through the ordinary registry: Spec("companion_profiles", ["profileId"], Mode.LWW, naturalPk = true, clock = "updatedAt") LWW because a profile is edited over time and the newer edit should win. Natural key because profileId is a portable UUID. Room v4 -> v5, additive, verbatim generated SQL, schema JSON committed, migration test written. The bespoke companion sync is retired: syncCompanion, companionFile, companionMediaFile, CompanionSync, decideCompanion, CompanionClash and pendingCompanionClash are all deleted. Two independent reasons. It keyed companion files PER CAR - "the paid companion IS the car" - which is MIDNIGHT AI's CLAUDE.md and has been stale here since the port. And with named profiles a "two companions met" clash is meaningless: two profiles simply coexist. All of it existed to force ONE identity across devices, which is precisely the constraint being removed. The active profile is device-local and deliberately never syncs. Switching it materialises that profile into CompanionProfile's existing flat keys, so AriaBrain, LiveSessionController and GeminiLiveSession keep reading identity exactly where they always have and needed no changes at all. 6fb493d · 3 files
Ticket 10's rulings were decided and never implemented - SyncEngine had 19 Spec registrations and none were ledger or pantry, so nothing ledger-side has ever synced. This implements the safe half and explains why the other half is deliberately still missing. ingested_files now syncs: LWW on the natural key driveFileId, clock lastAttemptAt. No syncId column is added; ticket 03 already strips the positional acc=N; prefix, so the stored id is identical on both devices for the same file. That is most of the value on its own - a second device skips fetch AND hash for a file the first one already handled, not merely the parse. ledger_transactions is deliberately NOT registered, and this is a correction to ticket 10 rather than an omission. That resolution justified UNION entirely on "transactions are immutable once committed". They are not: ticket 03/04's replace flow hard-deletes a file's rows when its Drive file is replaced in place. UNION has no delete action at all, so the next pass would re-download the still-present remote rows, find their syncIds absent locally, re-insert them and re-upload the resurrected set - silently double-counted money on the one table section 4's gate exists to protect, through a path the gate never sees because sync runs long after it. The tombstone pattern car_tasks and places use cannot rescue UNION either. It works there precisely BECAUSE they are LWW, where a newer deleted = 1 wins as an ordinary edit; under UNION an existing local row is never updated, so a soft-delete would never propagate. UNION and delete-propagation are mutually exclusive here, and ticket 10 explicitly rejected LWW. Kevin's call: defer the table to a tombstone ticket of its own rather than overturn a ruling inside a commit whose purpose was registration. The sync trigger is decoupled from the voice assistant. Its only caller was AriaForegroundService's engine-on gated loop, and that service starts only from the Settings assistant toggle, which defaults OFF - so ledger and pantry data would have synced only while the voice assistant happened to be running. That contradicts ticket 07's ruling that ledger, pantry and fleet work regardless of that toggle, and it is the same shape as L12. MainActivity.onResume now triggers it too; the service's own call stays, it was insufficient rather than wrong. Three review findings fixed: Retry exhaustion logs and skips instead of throwing an unreported IllegalStateException, per the resolution - but syncTable and syncFile now return Boolean and syncNow counts a skip as a failure. Without that, a table that never uploaded left `failures` at zero and the driver-facing string still read "Synced with your Google Drive." A sharded table reports failure if any shard was skipped, and still attempts every other shard first. DriveAuth.accessTokenOrNull ran OUTSIDE syncNow's try/catch. It bridges a Play Services Task and resumes with an exception on a genuine failure rather than returning null, so that throw escaped syncNow, escaped the caller's launch, and reached a root Job with no handler - a process crash. Harmless while the only caller was a periodic loop behind an off-by-default toggle; not harmless once a foreground resume calls it unconditionally. Both guards now sit inside. The foreground trigger built a fresh CoroutineScope inside onResume - no owner, no cancellation, a new one every resume, which is the anti-pattern the repo's vendored structured-concurrency skill names. Handing over the Activity's scope would be worse in a different way: rotating mid-pass would cancel a Drive upload. A sync pass is process work, so SyncEngine owns one SupervisorJob scope for the process lifetime and callers pass no scope at all. 71 unit tests, 0 failures. NOT verified: none of sync/ has still ever executed. Every claim here is traced from source. The first real two-device run is where it gets found out, and that has not happened. Every document date displayed a day early west of UTC
no ticket
1f1fa92 · 7 files
A receipt printed 04/18/2026 rendered as "Apr 17, 2026" on the A17K, and the ledger had been doing the same to every transaction date since it shipped. Every ingestion path normalises a parsed calendar date to UTC midnight - DbsStatementParser, BofaStatementParser, LedgerStatementAgent and PantryReceiptAgent all call atStartOfDay(ZoneOffset.UTC). Dates.kt then rendered through ZoneId.systemDefault(). At UTC-5, midnight on the 18th is 19:00 on the 17th, so the printed date and the displayed date disagreed by a day for anyone west of Greenwich. The values are date-only by construction - there is no time of day on a statement line - so the fix is to read them back in the zone they were written in. New documentDate/documentDateCompact do that, and the three call sites that render UTC-midnight values now use them: the ledger stream row, the pantry receipt header, and the get_transactions voice tool. Deliberately NOT a blanket change to shortDate/compactDate. Those same two formatters are also used on real instants - CodeEvent.timestamp, ServiceRecord.date and BuildEntry.date are System.currentTimeMillis() captures - and on MaintenanceItem.lastDoneDate, which LiveToolbox.parseIsoDate normalises to LOCAL midnight. All of those are correct in the device's zone and would have been broken by rendering them in UTC. Eight of the eleven call sites were already right; only three were wrong. Two regression tests. One asserts the property rather than a fixed string - the rendered date equals the date that was parsed - so it holds in whatever zone the test JVM runs in. The other pins the output across Pacific/Midway (UTC-11) and Pacific/Kiritimati (UTC+14), the extremes where a local-zone renderer lands on the day before and the day after. Verified on device (CPH2471): the receipt now reads Apr 18, 2026 against a printed 04/18/2026, and the ledger rows read Apr 27 / 19 / 11 / 5 against printed 27, 19, 11, 05 Apr. Those same rows read Apr 26 / 18 / 10 before this change. 71 unit tests, 0 failures. Found by rendering ticket 09's pantry screen on hardware. Nothing in compile, 71 tests, or two senior-dev reviews had surfaced it, because a date one day off still looks like a date. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

A fixture that reaches the LLM and reconciles, and the + bug it found
no ticket
bb7c5a7 · 5 files
Every fixture that fell through to the LLM was built to FAIL the reconciliation gate, so IngestMethod.LLM_RECONCILED had never been produced and the ledger's "read by AI" provenance label had never rendered anywhere. `unrecognized_reconciling.pdf` is the missing case: a layout neither deterministic parser claims, printing a net movement that equals the sum of its own signed lines, so a faithful extraction passes the gate and a dropped or hallucinated line does not. It is generated by tools/make_ledger_fixture.py rather than checked in as an opaque blob. The earlier fixtures came from ReportLab, which is not installed here and is not worth a dependency for one file, so the script writes an uncompressed PDF directly. The printed total is derived from the rows, never typed - a fixture whose own total is a typo would test the opposite of what it is for. The unit test guards both halves of the premise: that it really does fall through, and that neither parser's recognition marker can creep into it later and silently stop it testing the LLM path. Then it found a real bug on its first device run. The first cut printed its credits and total with a leading plus, the way statements actually do, and quarantined every time with "doesn't print a clear total to verify against". MONEY_RE was `^(-?)...` - it accepted a leading minus and rejected a leading plus. The model faithfully echoed the document's own formatting into statedTotal, parseMoneyCents threw, and the gate refused. That was a false negative, not a safety property. `+1,025.00` is not ambiguous; it is the same value stated explicitly, and any statement printing it would have quarantined forever. MONEY_RE now accepts it. MONEY_TOKEN_RE is deliberately left as `-?`. It only locates candidates for parseMoneyCents to validate, and a leading plus falls outside the match, so `+3,200.00` yields `3,200.00` and parses to the same cents. Widening it would move token boundaries in the deterministic parsers to buy nothing. The fixture itself stays unsigned. It exists to exercise a SUCCESSFUL reconciliation, and a fixture that also tested sign syntax would report a regression in one as a failure of the other. Verified on device (CPH2471): "Scan finished: 1 imported", and the "read by AI" label rendering for the first time beside genuinely LLM-extracted rows. A second currency appeared alongside the SGD account, correctly stacked with "no exchange rate is applied", and its balance reads "not stated" rather than 0.00 because the document prints no running balance. 46 unit tests, 0 failures. NOT verified on device: the + fix itself. It is covered by direct unit tests against parseMoneyCents, but no statement printing a plus has been run through a real extraction - that would be another billed call to prove a path the tests already pin. Resolves the design-language decision that blocked four UI tickets. ui/ has been a clean slate since the pivot killed city-pop; this is the first thing in it that is not a placeholder. Instrument is a retuning of Material 3's token layer, not a bespoke system. M3 keeps its components, touch targets, accessibility semantics and dynamic type; only colour, shape and type roles change. That is deliberately the opposite of Midnight AI, where AriaColors/AriaType/AriaDimens were built from scratch and every screen had to know about them. Three overrides do the work. The shape scale is flattened to near-zero, which is the single most load-bearing change: M3's 8-28dp radii and card-first habit cost vertical space and soften exactly the quality being sought. 2dp survives on the largest roles only because at 0dp a sheet has no visible edge against a near-black ground. Monospace covers anything numeric - Compose has no font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums, so picking a mono family is the mechanism for aligning digits down a column, not a style preference. And there is one accent; secondary and tertiary are neutrals. LegionSemantics sits outside ColorScheme because Material has no vocabulary for money or provenance, and squatting on tertiary would lie about that role's meaning and break when a component reads it for its own purposes. Two calls inside it are deliberate and easy to mistake for oversights: debit resolves to plain onSurface, since most statement rows are debits and colouring them all red turns signal into noise and hides the rare credit; and estimated is a guardrail rather than styling per CLAUDE.md §4 rule five, so an explicit label always carries the meaning and colour only reinforces it - colour alone fails in greyscale and for colour-blind users. themes.xml was Theme.Material.Light.NoActionBar, which flashed white on every cold start against a near-black app. It now matches the Compose ground, with colors.xml holding the one duplicated value since the launch window resolves before any Compose code runs. Dynamic colour is declined: it would hand the signal hue to the wallpaper and the signal is the identity. Verification: compileDebugKotlin -Pnokey green. It codifies what was previously implicit in the README: the pivot's locked decisions as a table, and the reconciliation gate as the one core architectural rule (deterministic-first, sum to the document's own stated total or quarantine, Long cents, provenance tags, and anything the document does not state is an estimate excluded from the gate). It also names the rules that are DEAD - frame-clock motion, AriaColors, city-pop, billing, AOSP 8-10 - because those were the bulk of the old guardrails and a reviewer will otherwise enforce them against the archive. memory/MEMORY.md is state only, 78 lines. Three things it records that were not written down anywhere: .claude/plans/wiggly-beaming-quasar.md does not exist (both READMEs cite it as the ledger+pantry design; .claude/ was never committed and did not survive the machine port), dev did not exist in this repo so the port landed straight on main, and nothing has ever run on a device. memory/library/ is all 21 shelves copied from MIDNIGHT_AI, each given a LIVE / PARTLY LIVE / FROZEN banner, with INDEX.md rewritten to carry a status column. Only decisions.md, lessons.md and parts of playbook-coding.md govern LEGION; playbook-coding got a section-by-section table since it splits both ways. The other 16 are frozen car-launcher history, kept as reference for why something was built a certain way, never as current blockers or backlog. The six agent defs are rewritten for a phone-only aspect-based app. bug-hunter now ranks data-integrity and silent-failure findings above all else (there is no crash reporting - MidnightEvents is Log.d only - so a swallowed exception is invisible in the field). analyst is non-optional for anything touching money or ingestion. librarian leads with the 2026-07-29 fabrication incident and a rule against filing LEGION facts into frozen shelves. business and marketing move to .claude/agents-parked/ with a README: there is no commercial model, so both seats would produce plausible work against a dead premise. settings.local.json is gitignored as per-machine; the shared agent defs are not. Add pantry aspect: LLM-vision receipt ingestion with reconciliation gate
no ticket
5099947 · 22 files
Grocery receipt photos have no deterministic layout the way bank statements do, so LLM vision is the primary path here, not a fallback - but the same reconciliation discipline applies: extracted line-item totals must sum exactly to the receipt's own printed total or the whole receipt quarantines, nothing written. Per-item macro estimates (calories/protein/carbs/fat) are never part of that check and are surfaced as estimates only, never fact. Extends SubAgent.kt with an optional inline image part (reused capability, not a one-off HTTP call). Replaces the old PhotoAlbumStore with ingestion-only PantryPhotoStore. Adds import_receipt/ list_recent_groceries/get_grocery_spend voice tools and a placeholder PantryImportActivity. Room v2->v3 with a verbatim, schema-matched migration. 8 new tests (19 total), all green.

Ledger port: bank-statement ingestion (deterministic-first, LLM fallback)
no ticket
cacfc34 · 32 files
Ports Project Andromeda's duo_ledger.bronze layer (Bank of America + DBS statement parsers, both with balance-continuity reconciliation) to Kotlin, plus a new LLM fallback for unrecognized layouts that enforces the same reconciliation principle before accepting anything - per the pivot's "LLM ingests behind a deterministic reconciliation gate, else quarantine" rule, applied here as the fallback path rather than the primary one (Kevin's explicit call, deterministic stays primary). Room: LedgerTransaction/LedgerTransactionDao, CarDatabase v1->v2 with a verbatim migration. Money stored as Long cents, not Double - existing BuildEntry/ServiceRecord use Double for a personal spend log, but ledger's entire reconciliation gate depends on exact equality checks that Double breaks via binary rounding. Every row tagged DETERMINISTIC or LLM_RECONCILED, never silently indistinguishable. Real technical finding along the way: PdfBox-Android (needed for DBS's per-word-coordinate column classification, which Android has no built-in equivalent for) ships its fonts/glyphlists as Android assets, unreachable from a plain JVM unit test - confirmed by actually running the spike test before porting the rest of the parser, not assuming it would work. Added Robolectric (test-only) to shadow AssetManager; the spike then verified real coordinate extraction against a generated fixture, matching the fixture generator's known column positions exactly. Also added .gitattributes (missing since the original scaffold) - verified byte-for-byte that Git's binary auto-detection had already protected the new PDF fixtures from LF/CRLF corruption, then locked it down explicitly rather than continuing to rely on the heuristic alone. 11 tests, 5 fixture PDFs (generated via Andromeda's own reportlab tooling for parity), all green: ./gradlew compileDebugKotlin -Pnokey and testDebugUnitTest both BUILD SUCCESSFUL. Voice tools: import_statement (UI-scoped, opens LedgerImportActivity), get_balance, list_recent_transactions. Not in scope (nothing to port - Andromeda's silver/gold/categorization/fx packages are empty stubs): spend-by-category, FX conversion, insights.
